source_text: aliam illi regulam praetendo: sicut naturalia, ita rationalia esse debere in deo omnia. exigo rationem bonitatis, quia nec aliud quid bonum haberi liceat, quod non rationaliter bonum sit, nedum ut ipsa bonitas inrationalis deprehendatur. facilius malum, cui rationis aliquid adfuerit, pro bono habebitur quam ut bonum ratone desertum non pro malo iudicetur. nego rationalem bonitatem\', dei Marcionis iam hoc primo, quod in salutem processerit; hominis alieni. scio dicturos atquin hanc esse principalem \' et perfectam bonitatem, cum sine ullo debito familiaritatis iri extraneos uoluntaria et libera effundatur, secundum quam inimicos quoque nostros et hoc nomine iam extraneos diligere iubeamur. cur ergo non a primordio hominem respexit. a primordio extraneum? cessando praeiudicauit cum extraneo nihil sibi esse. ceterum disciplinam diligendi extraneum uel inimicum antecessit praeceptum diligendi proximum tamquam te ipsum. quod etsi ex lege creatoris, et tu quoque illud excipere debebis, ut a Christo non destructum, sed potius exstructum. nam quo magis proximum diligas, diligere iuberis inimicum et extraneum. exaggeratio est debitae bonitatis exactio indebitae. antecedit autem debita indebitam, ut principalis, ut dignior, ut ministra et comite sua [id est indebita] prior. igitur cum prima bonitatis ratio sit in rem suam exhiberi ex iustitia, secunda autem in alienam ex redundantia iustitiae super scribarum et Pharisaeorum, quale est secundam ei rationem referri, cui deficit prima, non habenti proprium hominem ac per hoc quoque exiguae? porro exigua, quae suum non habuit, quomodo in alienum redundauit? exhibe principalem rationem, et tunc uindica sequentem. nulla res sine ordine rationalis potest uindicari; tanto abest, ut ratio ipsa in aliquo ordinem amittat. sit nunc et a secundo gradu incipiens ratio bonitatis, in extraneum scilicet: nec secundus illi gradus ratione constabit, alio modo destructus. tunc enim rationalis habebitur uel secunda in extraneum bonitas, si sine iniuria eius operetur, cuius est res. quamcumque bonitatem iustitia prima efficit rationalem. sicut in principali gradu, cum in rem suam exhibetur, rationalis erit si iusta sit, sic et in extraneum rationalis uideri poterit, si non sit iniusta. ceterum qualis bonitas quae per iniuriam constat, et quidem pro extraneo? fortasse enim pro domestico aliquatenus rationalis habeatur bonitas iniuriosa. pro extraneo uero, cui nec proba legitime deberetur, qua ratione tam iniusta rationalis defendetur? quid enim iniustius, quid iniquius et improbius quam ita alieno benefacere seruo, ut domino eripiatur, ut alii uindicetur, ut aduersus caput domini subornetur, et quidem, quod indignius, in ipsa adhuc domo domini, de ipsius adhuc horreis uiuens, sub ipsius adhuc plagis tremens? talis adsertor etiam damnaretur in saeculo, nedum plagiator. non aliter ** deus Marcionis, inrumpens in alienum mundum, eripiens deo hominem, patri filium, educatori aluminum, domino famulum, ut eum efficiat deo impium, patri inreligiosum, educatori ingratum, domino nequam. oro te, si rationalis bonitas talem facit, qualem faceret inrationalis? non putem impudentiorem quam qui in aliena aqua alii deo tingitur, ad alienum caelum alii deo expanditur, in aliena terra alii deo sternitur, super alienum panem alii deo gratiarum actionibus fungitur, de alienis bonis ob alium deum nomine elemosynae et dilectionis operatur. quis iste deus tam bonus, ut homo ab illo malus fiat, tam propitius, ut alium illi deum, et dominum quidem ipsius, faciat iratum?
pass_a_gloss: I propose to him another rule: just as natural things, so also rational things ought to be in God. I demand a reason for goodness, because no other thing can be considered good unless it is rationally good, much less that goodness itself be found irrational. It will be easier for evil, to which some reason has been added, to be considered good than that good, deserted by reason, not be judged evil. I deny rational goodness to Marcion's God, first because he proceeded to the salvation of a foreign man; I know they will say that this is the principal and perfect goodness, because it is voluntarily and freely poured out on foreigners without any debt of familiarity, according to which we are also commanded to love our enemies, who are already foreigners to us by this name. Why, then, did he not regard man from the beginning, from the beginning a foreigner? By ceasing, he prejudged that he had nothing to do with the foreigner. Moreover, the discipline of loving a foreigner or enemy preceded the command to love one's neighbor as oneself. Although this is from the law of the Creator, you also ought to accept it, as not destroyed by Christ, but rather built upon. For the more you love your neighbor, the more you are commanded to love your enemy and foreigner. The exacting of debt is an exaggeration of owed goodness. But owed goodness precedes unowed goodness, as principal, as more worthy, as minister and companion to its own, that is, unowed goodness, which comes first. Therefore, when the first reason for goodness is to exhibit it to one's own out of justice, and the second is to exhibit it to a foreigner out of the abundance of justice, what kind of second reason can be attributed to one who lacks the first, and does not have his own man, and therefore is also deficient? Furthermore, what is deficient, which did not have its own, how did it overflow into a foreigner? Show the principal reason, and then vindicate the subsequent one. No thing can be vindicated without order; so much so that reason itself does not lose order in anything. Let the reason for goodness now begin from the second grade, namely, in the foreigner: nor will the second grade of reason be consistent for him, having been destroyed in another way. For then rational goodness will be considered, or second goodness towards a foreigner, if it operates without injury to him whose thing it is. Whatever goodness justice first effects is rational. Just as in the principal grade, when it is exhibited to one's own, it will be rational if it is just, so also in a foreigner it can be seen as rational if it is not unjust. But what kind of goodness is it that consists through injury, and indeed for a foreigner? Perhaps, indeed, goodness that is injurious can be considered rational for a domestic servant to some extent. But for a foreigner, to whom not even legitimate goodness is owed, by what reason can such unjust goodness be defended as rational? What is more unjust, more iniquitous, and more wicked than to do good to a foreign servant in such a way that it is stolen from the master, vindicated to another, and suborned against the master's head, and indeed, what is more shameful, while still living in the master's house, from the master's stores, trembling under the master's blows? Such a defender would even be condemned in the world, not to mention the plagiarist. Not otherwise does Marcion's God, bursting into a foreign world, stealing man from God, son from father, pupil from teacher, servant from master, so that he makes him impious to God, irreligious to father, ungrateful to teacher, wicked to master. I ask you, if rational goodness makes one such, what would irrational goodness do? I do not think anyone is more shameless than one who is baptized in another's water to another god, expands to another god's heaven, is laid out on another god's earth, performs thanksgiving actions to another god over another's bread, and operates with another's goods in the name of charity and love for another god. What kind of god is so good that man becomes evil from him, so propitious that he makes another god, and indeed the master of him, angry?

choices.why: goodness that is due or owed
goodness that is not due or owed

pass_b_english: I set another rule before him: just as natural things are, so rational things ought to be in God. I demand a rational basis for goodness, because nothing else can count as good unless it is rationally good—much less can goodness itself be found irrational. It would be easier for evil, once some reason attaches to it, to pass as good than for good, deserted by reason, to escape being judged evil. I deny rational goodness to Marcion's God, first of all because he proceeded to the salvation of a foreign man. I know they will say this is the principal and perfect goodness, since it is poured out voluntarily and freely on strangers without any debt of kinship—precisely the standard by which we are commanded to love our enemies, who are already strangers to us by that very name. Why then did he not regard man from the beginning, from the beginning a stranger? By holding back, he prejudged that he had nothing to do with the stranger. Moreover, the discipline of loving a stranger or enemy preceded the command to love your neighbor as yourself. Even though that command comes from the Creator's law, you must accept it too, since Christ did not destroy it but built upon it. For the more you love your neighbor, the more you are commanded to love your enemy and the stranger. Exacting what is owed is an exaggeration of due goodness. But due goodness precedes undue goodness—as principal, as more worthy, as minister and companion to its own, that is, undue goodness, which comes first. Therefore, when the first reason for goodness is to show it to one's own out of justice, and the second is to show it to a foreigner out of the overflow of justice beyond the scribes and Pharisees, what kind of second reason can be assigned to one who lacks the first, who does not have his own man, and is therefore deficient? Furthermore, how did what is deficient, which never had its own, overflow into a foreigner? Produce the principal reason, and then vindicate the subsequent one. Nothing can be vindicated without rational order; so far is it from reason itself losing order in anything. Let the reason for goodness now begin from the second grade, namely toward the foreigner: nor will that second grade hold together rationally for him, since it has been destroyed another way. For only then will the second goodness toward a foreigner count as rational if it operates without injury to the one whose property it is. Whatever goodness justice first establishes is rational. Just as in the principal grade, when it is shown to one's own, it will be rational if it is just, so also toward a foreigner it can appear rational if it is not unjust. But what sort of goodness consists through injustice, and that for a foreigner? Perhaps injurious goodness might be considered rational to some extent for a household servant. But for a foreigner, to whom not even legitimate goodness is owed, by what reason can such unjust goodness be defended as rational? What is more unjust, more iniquitous, more wicked than to benefit a foreign servant in such a way that he is stolen from his master, claimed for another, and suborned against his master's head—and, what is more shameful, while still living in the master's house, eating from the master's stores, trembling under the master's blows? Such an advocate would be condemned even in the world, let alone the plagiarist. In no other way does Marcion's God, bursting into a foreign world, snatch man from God, son from father, pupil from teacher, servant from master, so that he makes him impious toward God, irreligious toward father, ungrateful toward teacher, wicked toward master. I ask you: if rational goodness produces such a man, what would irrational goodness produce? I cannot think of anyone more shameless than the one who is baptized in another's water for another god, ascends to another god's heaven, is laid out on another god's earth, offers thanksgiving over another's bread to another god, and operates with another's goods in the name of charity and love for another god. What kind of god is so good that man becomes evil from him, so favorable that he makes another god—indeed his own master—angry?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex logical structure of Tertullian's argument regarding 'rational goodness' (ratio bonitatis) and the distinction between 'owed' (debita) and 'unowed' (indebita) goodness. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin source. Pass B correctly includes the phrase 'beyond the scribes and Pharisees' (super scribarum et Pharisaeorum) which Pass A omitted. All scripture-alluded concepts are handled correctly.
